newsitem.title: USA: Summit will urge China to keep Hong Kong promises.
newsitem.headline: Summit will urge China to keep Hong Kong promises.

text.p: With China poised to take control of Hong Kong in less than two weeks, a summit of industrialised nations in Denver this weekend is expected to urge Beijing to honour promises to preserve the territory's autonomy, U.S. officials say.

Leaders of the "Summit of the Eight," combining the Group of Seven industrial giants with Russia, hold their annual economic summit from Friday to Sunday in this mile-high Rocky Mountain city and foreign policy is likely to be as important as the more traditional fare of world financial issues.

One foreign policy concern involves Hong Kong, the British colony that reverts to Chinese sovereignty on July 1 after more than 150 years of British rule. The United States and its allies have urged China to let Hong Kong retain its political freedom and open economy in line with the obligations outlined in the 1984 Basic Agreement between China and Britain.

President Bill Clinton's national security adviser Sandy Berger said in a pre-summit briefing that the eight leaders will discuss their "shared expectation that China will fulfil those expectations and that the international community will watch very carefully to see if that is taking place."

U.S. officials said an expression of concern for Hong Kong's future will be included in a final communique issued by the G7 nations -- the United States, Japan, France, Britain, Italy, Germany and Canada -- and Russia.

Denver, at the foot of the snow-capped Rocky Mountains, is draped in flags as it braces for the onslaught of eight delegations, complete with gridlock-inducing motorcades, and thousands of journalists ready to cover every nuance of this 23rd annual meeting.

Most of the summit will be staged in the bookish confines of the Denver Public Library, but the leaders will break free for a "Saturday Night at the Summit" extravaganza featuring performers such as Lyle Lovett, Amy Grant, Michael Bolton and Kool and the Gang.
Summit spouses will have lunch on Saturday at a restaurant on top of a 10,700 foot (3,250-metre) mountain.
Clinton will lay out his agenda for the summit in a speech on Thursday shortly after arriving in Denver.

The United States, enjoying a booming economy and declining budget deficit, has put out the word that it expects the summit to take a broader, foreign policy focus instead of concentrating on the traditional economic issues that have dominated past sessions, such as free trade agreements and budget deficits.
"It's not going to be like the G7 of old," said a White House official.

The participants are calling this a "Summit of the Eight" in a symbolic gesture to stress Russian integration with the group. President Boris Yeltsin will be excluded from only one financial-related meeting in three days of summitry.

Yeltsin, 66, missed last year's summit in Lyon, France, because of heart surgery. He comes to Denver in better physical and political shape but still presiding over a country with huge economic problems.
The leaders will also focus on attempts to build a durable peace in Bosnia and to rekindle the Middle East peace process.
But they will in addition make a major push to promote trade and investment in Africa to bring the sub-Sahara out of endemic poverty.

U.S. officials said they expected the eight to issue a statement pledging to coordinate their efforts to help Africa avoid the type of conflicts that have led to the slaughter of tens of thousands of people.
One issue expected to surface at bilateral meetings outside the summit is plans to invite new members to join NATO.

The United States said last week in defiance of its allies that it wanted to invite only three nations -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin negotiations to enter the Western security alliance.
France and Germany insist they will support Romania and Slovenia for membership despite the U.S. stance.
